text:
Recent work separates functional relationships from compatibility. [TREC 2025](https://trec-product-search.github.io/recommendations.html) distinguishes substitutes, complements, unrelated items, and “unable to assess”; complements further separate likely compatibility, unknown compatibility, and explicit incompatibility. This provides a useful diagnostic vocabulary without forcing uncertain judgments. [ECCR (2024)](https://www.amazon.science/publications/eccr-explainable-and-coherent-complement-recommendation-based-on-large-language-models) argues that co-purchase alone does not establish meaningful complementarity; it generates explanations alongside recommendations and evaluates coherence through human judgments. Earlier [AMRule](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.13749) offers an interpretable precedent: compatibility rules derived from product descriptions and structured attributes. For this task, only rules supported by available titles/descriptions would apply.

Suggested adaptation: record relation type, compatibility status, and supporting text spans separately. Explicit model/interface mismatches can support incompatibility flags; missing specifications should produce “unknown.” Treat similar-function recommendations following historical interactions as potential redundancy, not proven unnecessary replacements: histories and timestamps do not establish current ownership, equipment availability, or replacement intent. Validate these probes against independently annotated qualitative examples, reporting agreement, precision of flagged cases, and abstention coverage; keep them separate from benchmark HR@10. Include ambiguous pairs and cases with missing specifications. [AbstentionBench (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09038) finds that stronger reasoning does not reliably solve abstention, and prompting alone remains insufficient—supporting explicit evidence requirements and evaluation of unknown decisions rather than trusting fluent explanations or self-reported confidence.
